screens.title: Data-Driven Scenarios: Scenario Outline & Data Tables
screens.narratorSegment: In Behavior-Driven Development we frequently need to verify the same behavior against several sets of data. This chapter teaches two compact Gherkin constructs that make that possible: Scenario Outline with Examples tables and inline Data Tables for step-level structured data. You will learn when to repeat a scenario and when to parametrize it; how placeholders in angle brackets map to columns in an Examples table; and how to pass tabular data directly into a step using a Data Table. The practical goal is to keep feature files DRY and readable while ensuring reliable, automated checks across multiple inputs. We'll use a simple calculator and a shopping-cart example to ground the ideas, and you'll see how step definitions receive typed values and table maps. By the end you will be able to replace duplicated scenarios with a Scenario Outline, pick Data Tables for single-step structures, and avoid common maintenance pitfalls such as oversized Examples tables or mismatched placeholders. Think of these tools as ways to move data closer to the behavior you describe, without losing clarity.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Data-Driven Scenarios
Data-Driven Scenarios
Use Scenario Outlines and Data Tables to express repeated behavior clearly and concisely.
In this lesson you'll learn to move from duplicated examples to parameterized scenarios, and when to prefer an Examples table versus a Data Table for a step. The patterns you learn reduce maintenance and make intent visible to both technical and non-technical stakeholders.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
A focused walk-through of examples, step definitions, and common pitfalls.
Explore Key Topics
Scenario Outline
Placeholders and Examples let one scenario cover many input combinations while remaining readable.
Data Table
Pass structured rows or maps to a single step, ideal for lists like cart items or permissions.
Step Definitions
Map placeholders and tables to typed method parameters or maps in step code.
Visual Concept
One Scenario
Placeholders are filled by Examples rows to create multiple executions.
One Step
A Data Table supplies structured rows to a single step action.
Step Code
Step defs parse typed parameters or maps depending on the input form.
Coming up
We will show a calculator Scenario Outline, a shopping-cart Data Table, Java step-def examples, and a user-registration activity you can implement.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand why data-driven scenarios matter and how to express them in Gherkin. First, you'll learn the purpose and benefits of Scenario Outlines: how placeholders and Examples tables reduce duplication and make intent clearer. Second, you will practice constructing Scenario Outlines with properly named placeholders and Examples rows so each execution maps to a distinct test case. Third, you'll learn when and how to use Data Tables inside a step to pass lists or maps of structured data, and how that keeps complex inputs close to the behavior they affect. Finally, you'll implement step definitions that parse values from both Examples and Data Tables, learning the typical patterns for typed parameters and conversion. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint so you can recall the pattern during authoring. These skills matter because they keep feature files readable for stakeholders while enabling reliable automation, reducing maintenance pain and avoiding hidden duplication.

screens.title: Why data-driven scenarios?
screens.narratorSegment: Data-driven scenarios exist to solve a simple but common problem: many behaviors follow the same steps but need to be validated against different inputs. Writing a separate scenario for each input creates repetition, bloated feature files, and more work when requirements change. Scenario Outlines address this by allowing a single scenario to run multiple times with different values supplied by an Examples table. This keeps the logical flow visible and minimizes duplication. Data Tables complement this approach when structured rows belong to a single step, such as adding multiple products to a cart or setting a user's permissions. A Data Table keeps the table close to the action that consumes it, improving readability for stakeholders who read the feature file. A common misconception is that more rows always equal better coverage; in practice, very large Examples tables harm readability and may indicate the need for fixtures or external data sources. Use Scenario Outlines for multiple, discrete permutations of a scenario, and Data Tables when the data is a structured argument to one step. The key takeaway is clarity: keep behavior first and data next to the action that uses it.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Scenario Outlines run one scenario many times with Examples; Data Tables pass structured, step-level data for lists or maps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Why data-driven scenarios?
Purpose and benefits
Reduce duplication, keep intent clear, and make test cases easy to audit.
  • Scenario Outlines remove repetition by parameterizing steps and using Examples rows for each input set.
  • Data Tables supply structured data to a single step, suitable for lists or maps such as cart items or permissions.
  • Both keep data near the behavior, improving readability for non-technical reviewers.
  • Watch out for oversized Examples tables; too many rows reduce clarity and hint that external fixtures may be appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Prefer Scenario Outlines for repeated scenario permutations; prefer Data Tables when an action needs structured rows or maps as input.

Concrete analogies and example
Think of a Scenario Outline as a recipe you run with different ingredients; the Examples table lists the ingredient sets. A Data Table is a shopping list supplied to a single cooking step.
Calculator Example (illustrative)
Feature: Calculator Addition
  Scenario Outline: Add two numbers
    Given I have entered <number1> into the calculator
    And I have entered <number2> into the calculator
    When I press add
    Then the result should be <expected_result>

    Examples:
      | number1 | number2 | expected_result |
      | 2       | 3       | 5               |
      | 10      | -5      | 5               |
Common misconception: Scenario Outlines are not a substitute for proper test design. They simplify permutations, but they do not replace thoughtful selection of representative cases or the use of external fixtures when many combinations are required.

screens.title: Scenario Outline mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: A Scenario Outline uses placeholders inside angle brackets that are replaced by values from an Examples table at run time. Each row in the Examples table creates one execution of the scenario, with column names matching placeholder names. This mapping is literal; placeholder names must exactly match the column header including case. For example, if you have placeholders number1 and number2, your Examples table must include columns named number1 and number2. The test runner substitutes the row values into the steps before step matching occurs, so from the step definition's perspective it sees a concrete step with typed parameters. The practical result is fewer scenario blocks and clearer test intent. A frequent beginner mistake is mixing up header names or adding extra whitespace; this causes the placeholder to remain unresolved. Another mistake is putting too many unrelated permutations in one Outline, which obscures intent. Use an Outline for closely related input permutations and keep edge cases in separate scenarios if they require different preconditions. Try to name placeholders descriptively so each Examples row reads like a test case summary. Scenario Outline mechanics means placeholders map directly to examples columns; each examples row produces a distinct scenario execution with substituted values.. In practical terms, placeholders, examples rows, and how cucumber executes them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Scenario Outline mechanics
How placeholders become values
Each Examples row yields one run with placeholders substituted before step matching.
1. Use angle-bracket placeholders like <item> in steps to indicate variable positions.
2. Add an Examples table whose column headers match placeholder names exactly.
3. Each table row becomes a separate execution and the test runner replaces placeholders with row values.
4. Step definitions receive parsed values as typed parameters according to their step annotations.
Common mistake

Mismatched header names or extra whitespace prevents substitution and causes runtime errors. Spell headers exactly.

Concrete example
Scenario Outline: Add two numbers
  Given I have entered <number1> into the calculator
  And I have entered <number2> into the calculator
  When I press add
  Then the result should be <expected_result>

  Examples:
    | number1 | number2 | expected_result |
    | 2       | 3       | 5               |
    | 1.5     | 2.5     | 4.0             |
Note how the table headers match the placeholders. If the header was Number1 instead of number1, the placeholder would not resolve and the runner would not substitute the values correctly.

screens.title: Step definitions for Scenario Outlines
screens.narratorSegment: When a Scenario Outline executes, each substituted step becomes a concrete step that the Cucumber runner matches against step definitions. In Java, Cucumber's expression language lets you use typed capture groups such as {double} or {int} in the annotation so the framework parses the string value and passes a typed parameter into your method. For example, a Given step that accepts a double will receive 2.5 as a double parameter. Implementations typically create or reuse a domain object — for instance, a Calculator instance — and then store or operate on the incoming value. It's important to initialize shared state in a way that works across repeated executions of the Outline; failing to reset state between examples can cause false positives or false negatives. Also be mindful of locale and decimal separators when parsing floating point values. When writing step definitions, keep them small and focused: one action per step, predictable parameter types, and clear error messages when parsing fails. That practice makes debugging failing rows straightforward and keeps the mapping between human-readable examples and automation behavior transparent. In practical terms, mapping placeholders to typed parameters in java/cucumber. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Step definitions for Outlines
Java example
A typical step definition accepts typed parameters using Cucumber expressions.
import io.cucumber.java.en.Given;

public class CalculatorSteps {
  private Calculator calculator;

  @Given("I have entered {double} into the calculator")
  public void iHaveEnteredNumberIntoTheCalculator(double number) {
    if (calculator == null) {
      calculator = new Calculator();
    }
    calculator.enter(number);
  }
}
This method receives the parsed double directly. If your Examples row contains 1.5, the method gets 1.5 as a double rather than a raw string.
Practical tips
  • Reset or reinstantiate state between Outline runs so rows don't share leftover data.
  • Choose typed capture groups to avoid manual parsing and conversion errors.
  • Keep step code small: parsing and delegating to domain helpers simplifies tests and maintenance.
Misconception

Putting heavy business logic inside step methods makes tests brittle. Prefer light parsing and delegate logic to domain helpers.

screens.title: Data Tables: purpose and formats
screens.narratorSegment: A Data Table is a multi-line step argument used when a single step needs a structured set of values. Use it for lists of items, configuration rows, or key-value maps that belong conceptually to one action. For example, adding multiple products to a cart fits naturally in a Data Table; each row describes one product with columns for name, quantity, and price. Data Tables are not intended to replace Scenario Outlines; they are complementary. The Outline repeats the scenario with different row values across runs, while a Data Table provides a single, structured input to a step during one execution. When you need multiple runs that differ only by top-level inputs, use an Examples table. When a step needs an internal list or mapping, use a Data Table. A common error is to overuse Examples tables for nested structures; that makes rows awkward to read and maintain. Keep the data shape aligned with the action: tables for grouped rows, outlines for multiple executions. This approach keeps feature files expressive and makes step implementation straightforward because the table maps to a list or a list of maps in code.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Data Tables
When to choose a Data Table
Structured rows for a single step action, like multiple cart items or permission rows.
Example: Shopping cart
When I add the following products to my cart:
  | Product Name | Quantity | Price |
  | Laptop       | 1        | 1200  |
  | Mouse        | 2        | 25    |
  | Keyboard     | 1        | 75    |
This table is an argument to the When step. The step implementation will typically convert it into a list of maps where keys are column headers and values are the row values.
Why not use an Examples table here?
An Examples table repeats the entire scenario. If the variation is internal to a single action, repeating scenarios is unnecessary and reduces readability. Use Data Tables to keep complex inputs local to the step.
Key Takeaway

Use Data Tables when a single step needs a structured list or map; use Examples to repeat the whole scenario with different top-level inputs.

screens.title: Parsing Data Tables in step code
screens.narratorSegment: When a step receives a Data Table, most frameworks provide an A P I to convert that table into language-friendly structures. In Cucumber-JVM you can accept io. cucumber. datatable. DataTable as a method parameter and call asMaps(String. class, String. class) to convert rows into a List of Maps where each map keys are the column headers. This pattern makes iterating rows straightforward: you read the product name, parse quantity and price, and call your domain method to add items to a cart. Since Data Tables are string-based, you must convert numeric strings to integers or doubles in your step code. A common beginner error is to assume the Data Table preserves types; it does not. Validate and convert carefully and fail fast with a clear message if parsing fails. Keep table handling focused in the step method and delegate domain operations such as cart. addProduct to dedicated classes. This separation makes tests readable and keeps parsing logic testable in isolation when needed. Parsing Data Tables in step code means use datatable.asmaps to get a list of maps; convert numeric strings to the expected types and delegate domain operations to helper classes.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Parsing Data Tables
Java step definition example
import io.cucumber.java.en.When;
import io.cucumber.datatable.DataTable;

public class ShoppingCartSteps {
  private ShoppingCart cart = new ShoppingCart();

  @When("I add the following products to my cart:")
  public void iAddTheFollowingProductsToMyCart(DataTable productsTable) {
    List> products = productsTable.asMaps(String.class, String.class);
    for (Map product : products) {
      String productName = product.get("Product Name");
      int quantity = Integer.parseInt(product.get("Quantity"));
      double price = Double.parseDouble(product.get("Price"));
      cart.addProduct(productName, quantity, price);
    }
  }
}
Key considerations
  • Data tables are strings by default; convert types explicitly and validate formats.
  • Use asMaps to preserve header-to-value mapping for readability and stability.
  • Delegate business logic to domain helpers so the step remains an adapter between Gherkin and code.
Pro tip

Include clear error messages on parsing failures so failing table rows point to the problematic values quickly.

screens.title: Examples table vs Data Table
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an Examples table and a Data Table comes down to intent. Use an Examples table when you want to repeat the whole scenario with different top-level inputs. Each row represents a distinct test case and the runner executes the scenario once per row. Use a Data Table when a single step needs structured rows or key-value mappings as input — the scenario runs once and the step consumes the table. A practical distinction: if your change requires altering preconditions or the flow, it's probably a separate scenario or a Scenario Outline. If your change is about items fed into one action, prefer a Data Table. Mistakes happen when people flatten nested structures into Examples columns, producing unreadable headers and many columns that are hard to scan. Another error is putting too many permutations in an Examples table that really belong in fixtures. Remember maintainability: keep each feature easy to read for stakeholders, and ensure your automation code parses the chosen structure reliably. Use clear column headers and descriptive placeholder names to make intent obvious. Examples table vs Data Table means examples repeat scenarios across rows; data tables supply structured rows to one step. pick based on whether you need multiple executions or structured input for one execution.. In practical terms, choose the right structure for your scenario. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Avoiding common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Working with Scenario Outlines and Data Tables introduces a few recurring pitfalls. First, inconsistent or misspelled placeholder names break substitution; always double-check header names and casing. Second, putting dozens of rows into an Examples table reduces readability and signals that the data may belong in external fixtures or seeded test data instead. Third, not resetting state between Outline executions can cause rows to interfere with each other, producing false positives or confusing failures. Fourth, treating Data Tables as typed objects without converting strings leads to parse errors; always convert and validate. Fifth, embedding UI implementation details into the feature makes it harder for non-technical stakeholders to understand the intent; keep features focused on behavior and let step code handle UI interaction details. Use a checklist when authoring: verify headers, limit table size, reset state, validate conversions, and keep behavior-first language. Doing this prevents common maintenance issues and preserves the readable nature of BDD specifications. fullNarratorScript:
In Behavior-Driven Development we frequently need to verify the same behavior against several sets of data. This chapter teaches two compact Gherkin constructs that make that possible: Scenario Outline with Examples tables and inline Data Tables for step-level structured data. You will learn when to repeat a scenario and when to parametrize it; how placeholders in angle brackets map to columns in an Examples table; and how to pass tabular data directly into a step using a Data Table. The practical goal is to keep feature files DRY and readable while ensuring reliable, automated checks across multiple inputs. We'll use a simple calculator and a shopping-cart example to ground the ideas, and you'll see how step definitions receive typed values and table maps. By the end you will be able to replace duplicated scenarios with a Scenario Outline, pick Data Tables for single-step structures, and avoid common maintenance pitfalls such as oversized Examples tables or mismatched placeholders. Think of these tools as ways to move data closer to the behavior you describe, without losing clarity.

By the end of this chapter you will understand why data-driven scenarios matter and how to express them in Gherkin. First, you'll learn the purpose and benefits of Scenario Outlines: how placeholders and Examples tables reduce duplication and make intent clearer. Second, you will practice constructing Scenario Outlines with properly named placeholders and Examples rows so each execution maps to a distinct test case. Third, you'll learn when and how to use Data Tables inside a step to pass lists or maps of structured data, and how that keeps complex inputs close to the behavior they affect. Finally, you'll implement step definitions that parse values from both Examples and Data Tables, learning the typical patterns for typed parameters and conversion. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint so you can recall the pattern during authoring. These skills matter because they keep feature files readable for stakeholders while enabling reliable automation, reducing maintenance pain and avoiding hidden duplication.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills and pitfalls to avoid. You will build Scenario Outlines for realistic cases like registration and arithmetic operations, and implement step definitions that accept typed values. You will also use Data Tables to represent multi-row inputs such as product lists, and convert those tables to language-native structures inside step code. Importantly, you will learn to spot signs that an Examples table has grown too large: if there are dozens of rows, readability suffers and the data may belong in an external fixture rather than the feature file. Another practical skill is matching placeholder names precisely to column headers; small typos cause runtime failures. These lessons help you maintain readable specifications that both product owners and developers can agree on. As a final milestone you will complete a short registration Scenario Outline covering valid and invalid inputs, reinforcing the mapping between human-readable scenarios and the automation implementation.

Data-driven scenarios exist to solve a simple but common problem: many behaviors follow the same steps but need to be validated against different inputs. Writing a separate scenario for each input creates repetition, bloated feature files, and more work when requirements change. Scenario Outlines address this by allowing a single scenario to run multiple times with different values supplied by an Examples table. This keeps the logical flow visible and minimizes duplication. Data Tables complement this approach when structured rows belong to a single step, such as adding multiple products to a cart or setting a user's permissions. A Data Table keeps the table close to the action that consumes it, improving readability for stakeholders who read the feature file. A common misconception is that more rows always equal better coverage; in practice, very large Examples tables harm readability and may indicate the need for fixtures or external data sources. Use Scenario Outlines for multiple, discrete permutations of a scenario, and Data Tables when the data is a structured argument to one step. The key takeaway is clarity: keep behavior first and data next to the action that uses it.

A Scenario Outline uses placeholders inside angle brackets that are replaced by values from an Examples table at run time. Each row in the Examples table creates one execution of the scenario, with column names matching placeholder names. This mapping is literal; placeholder names must exactly match the column header including case. For example, if you have placeholders number1 and number2, your Examples table must include columns named number1 and number2. The test runner substitutes the row values into the steps before step matching occurs, so from the step definition's perspective it sees a concrete step with typed parameters. The practical result is fewer scenario blocks and clearer test intent. A frequent beginner mistake is mixing up header names or adding extra whitespace; this causes the placeholder to remain unresolved. Another mistake is putting too many unrelated permutations in one Outline, which obscures intent. Use an Outline for closely related input permutations and keep edge cases in separate scenarios if they require different preconditions. Try to name placeholders descriptively so each Examples row reads like a test case summary. Scenario Outline mechanics means placeholders map directly to examples columns; each examples row produces a distinct scenario execution with substituted values.. In practical terms, placeholders, examples rows, and how cucumber executes them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a Scenario Outline executes, each substituted step becomes a concrete step that the Cucumber runner matches against step definitions. In Java, Cucumber's expression language lets you use typed capture groups such as {double} or {int} in the annotation so the framework parses the string value and passes a typed parameter into your method. For example, a Given step that accepts a double will receive 2.5 as a double parameter. Implementations typically create or reuse a domain object — for instance, a Calculator instance — and then store or operate on the incoming value. It's important to initialize shared state in a way that works across repeated executions of the Outline; failing to reset state between examples can cause false positives or false negatives. Also be mindful of locale and decimal separators when parsing floating point values. When writing step definitions, keep them small and focused: one action per step, predictable parameter types, and clear error messages when parsing fails. That practice makes debugging failing rows straightforward and keeps the mapping between human-readable examples and automation behavior transparent. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Data Table is a multi-line step argument used when a single step needs a structured set of values. Use it for lists of items, configuration rows, or key-value maps that belong conceptually to one action. For example, adding multiple products to a cart fits naturally in a Data Table; each row describes one product with columns for name, quantity, and price. Data Tables are not intended to replace Scenario Outlines; they are complementary. The Outline repeats the scenario with different row values across runs, while a Data Table provides a single, structured input to a step during one execution. When you need multiple runs that differ only by top-level inputs, use an Examples table. When a step needs an internal list or mapping, use a Data Table. A common error is to overuse Examples tables for nested structures; that makes rows awkward to read and maintain. Keep the data shape aligned with the action: tables for grouped rows, outlines for multiple executions. This approach keeps feature files expressive and makes step implementation straightforward because the table maps to a list or a list of maps in code.

When a step receives a Data Table, most frameworks provide an A P I to convert that table into language-friendly structures. In Cucumber-JVM you can accept io. cucumber. datatable. DataTable as a method parameter and call asMaps(String. class, String. class) to convert rows into a List of Maps where each map keys are the column headers. This pattern makes iterating rows straightforward: you read the product name, parse quantity and price, and call your domain method to add items to a cart. Since Data Tables are string-based, you must convert numeric strings to integers or doubles in your step code. A common beginner error is to assume the Data Table preserves types; it does not. Validate and convert carefully and fail fast with a clear message if parsing fails. Keep table handling focused in the step method and delegate domain operations such as cart. addProduct to dedicated classes. This separation makes tests readable and keeps parsing logic testable in isolation when needed. Parsing Data Tables in step code means use datatable.asmaps to get a list of maps; convert numeric strings to the expected types and delegate domain operations to helper classes.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Each row represents a distinct test case and the runner executes the scenario once per row. Use a Data Table when a single step needs structured rows or key-value mappings as input — the scenario runs once and the step consumes the table. A practical distinction: if your change requires altering preconditions or the flow, it's probably a separate scenario or a Scenario Outline. If your change is about items fed into one action, prefer a Data Table. Another error is putting too many permutations in an Examples table that really belong in fixtures.
